newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU, U.S. set to grapple over grain subsidies.
newsitem.headline: EU, U.S. set to grapple over grain subsidies.

text.p: The United States and Europe, the world's two farming superpowers, are poised next week to try to prevent a potential grain subsidy war adding to mounting transatlantic trade tensions, analysts said on Friday.

Talks in Brussels will focus on U.S. hostility to a recent European Union move to restore wheat export subsidies, prompted by bumper harvests that have sent world prices tumbling below the levels guaranteed to European farmers.

"Things don't look too good for the future. They are reverting to the subsidy policies of the 1980s," a veteran farm trade analyst said at Europe's largest annual grain fair held this year in Antwerp.
The EU, ending a year-long subsidy truce between Washington and Europe for wheat sales, resumed subsidised exports last month in the face of increasingly strident U.S. warnings.
U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman pledged last week to fight subsidies with subsidies if necessary to prevent the EU's "subsidised tentacles" distorting the world grain market.
Glickman's top trade adviser, Paul Drazek, said on Thursday he would travel to Europe to meet senior EU officials on the grain subsidies as well as other key agricultural issues.
But later in the day the EU's top farm official, Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler, dismissed the U.S. criticisms and suggested they had more to do with the U.S. presidential race.
"It perhaps also has something to do with the election campaign," he told an industry dinner in Antwerp on Thursday.
Analysts say the Clinton administration will be anxious to reassure farmers in key Midwest grain states that it is fighting for their interests in the run-up to the November poll.

Fischler noted that Washington had criticised Brussels when it took the rare step of taxing wheat exports as prices soared to records earlier this year. Now that the opposite was happening, the U.S. was complaining again, he said.

But in an apparent bid to soothe Washington, Fischler reiterated that the EU would continue to respect a 1994 world farm trade accord to open markets and cut the use of trade distorting subsidies. And he promised that even with its wheat subsidies, the EU would not be undercutting U.S. prices.
Some among the nearly 2,000 delegates were perplexed at the growing transatlantic criticism.
"It's rather surprising given the U.S. has a relatively small crop this year," Steve Thornhill, Economics Director of the U.K. Home Grown Cereals Authority, told Reuters.
It seemed to reflect worries about what could be a record EU grain harvest this year and positioning for the following season when much bigger U.S. output is likely, he added.
The grain subsidy tensions swell a growing list of transatlantic trade disputes stretching far beyond agriculture.
The EU on Friday moved formally to achieve creation of a World Trade Organisation panel on the U.S. Helms-Burton Cuban investment law which Brussels argues violates trade rules.
For its part Washington has complained that an EU ban on imports of hormone-treated meat breaks free-trade rules. It also says EU banana import rules are discriminatory.
And it is uneasy about a threatened European consumer boycott of a new strand of genetically modified soybeans that the United States says are perfectly safe.
